summaries.summary: Equations are important but challenging for machine learning because most occur only once, while useful representations could benefit scientific literature analysis, retrieval, and navigation.
The paper proposes equation embeddings (EqEmb), an unsupervised approach treating each equation as a singleton word represented using surrounding text representations.
Figure FIGREF1 shows an article snippet BIBREF0 with a unique arXiv equation whose surrounding text enables an embedding that finds related equations and words.
EqEmbs build on exponential family embeddings BIBREF1 to include equations as singleton observations and model variables, symbols and operators using word and equation contexts.
EqEmbs were studied on four arXiv collections covering NLP, IR, AI and ML, including INLINEFORM0 87k equations, and provided better models and coherent semantic representations.
Word embeddings introduced in BIBREF2, BIBREF3 and variants BIBREF4, BIBREF5, BIBREF6, BIBREF7 use latent feature vectors, and EqEmb extends word embeddings to equations.
Prior equation representations include the symbol layout tree BIBREF8, and this work also falls within mathematical language processing (MLP) BIBREF9.

EqEmb are based on word embeddings BIBREF5 or Bernoulli embeddings (b-embs) BIBREF1, which model a word INLINEFORM0 given context INLINEFORM1 using INLINEFORM7 dimensional embedding and context vectors.
B-emb is an exponential family embedding model where the conditional distribution is a Bernoulli: DISPLAYFORM0.
The parameter INLINEFORM0 is defined using the word embedding INLINEFORM1 and the word context INLINEFORM2 vectors: DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is the logistic function.
Given a dataset of words and equations, EqEmb models derive semantic representations of equations by expanding word context to include equations in a possibly larger window.
Embeddings are assigned to words (INLINEFORM0, INLINEFORM1) and equations (INLINEFORM2, INLINEFORM3), with an objective containing conditionals over observed words and equations: DISPLAYFORM0.
The objective sums conditionals over observed words (INLINEFORM0) and observed equations (INLINEFORM1), using interaction INLINEFORM4 and feature vector INLINEFORM5 terminology.
The context of word INLINEFORM1 includes original context INLINEFORM2 and equations INLINEFORM3 in a possibly larger window, called the word-equation context window.
Both conditionals are Bernoulli distributions, and the first conditional over words in the collection has parameter DISPLAYFORM0.
The word context function is DISPLAYFORM0.
This function encompasses words in original word context INLINEFORM0 and equations INLINEFORM1 appearing in a possibly larger window INLINEFORM2.
The second objective term sums log conditional probabilities of each equation, with parameter DISPLAYFORM0.
Equation context INLINEFORM0 contains words in a context window around the equation: DISPLAYFORM0.

Equation context can have a larger window than word context, and equation feature vectors INLINEFORM0 are only associated with the first objective term containing words where the equation appears in larger context INLINEFORM1.

Figure FIGREF1 shows that with word context size INLINEFORM0 and context window size of 4 (INLINEFORM1), modeling "embedding" ignores equations, while word-equation context window size INLINEFORM2 =16 includes the equation feature vector.

Equation unit embeddings (EqEmb-U) treat equations as sentences of variables, symbols and operators called units, tokenized using BIBREF8 into syntax layout tree (SLT) tuples, with Figure FIGREF11 showing three equations.
Each equation INLINEFORM0 is a sequence of equation units INLINEFORM1, INLINEFORM2, and each equation unit INLINEFORM3 receives interaction INLINEFORM4 and feature INLINEFORM5 vectors.

Word INLINEFORM0 context includes original context INLINEFORM1 and equation units INLINEFORM2 from equations in the word-equation context window, while unit context INLINEFORM3 contains surrounding units in small window INLINEFORM4: DISPLAYFORM0.
The objective is over two conditionals, one for each context type: DISPLAYFORM0.
The two parameters are DISPLAYFORM0.
Equation-level representations are defined by averaging the representations of their constituent units: DISPLAYFORM0.

Stochastic gradient descent with Adagrad BIBREF10 fits vectors, with gradients split into non-zero entries INLINEFORM0 and zero entries INLINEFORM1, exact gradients for non-zero points, subsampling for zero data points, and early stopping based on validation accuracy.
EqEmb performance was studied on arXiv articles, where EqEmb models provide better fits than existing embedding approaches and infer meaningful semantic relationships between equations and words.

Proposed models are compared with Bernoulli embeddings (b-emb) BIBREF1, continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) BIBREF5, Distributed Memory version of Paragraph Vector (PV-DM) BIBREF11 and Global Vectors (GloVe) BIBREF6.
Datasets are arXiv scientific articles in LaTeX from NLP, IR, AI and ML, filtered by primary and secondary categories: cs.cl, cs.ir, cs.ai and stat.ml, stat.co, stat.me or cs.lg.

Table TABREF22 shows documents, unique words, equations and equation units; display equations were enumerated in LaTeX, and the empirical study used a random subset of 2k singletons plus all equations occurring more than once, while qualitative analysis used all equations.
Words were extracted by tokenizing articles using the NLTK package BIBREF12 and restricting vocabulary to noun phrases and adjectives.
Vocabulary selection involved removing common stopwords.
Vocabulary selection involved treating the top 25 most frequent words as stop words and removing them.
Vocabulary selection included words whose term frequency is greater than or equal to 10 and whose character length is greater than or equal to 4.
Vocabulary selection included the top 50 most frequent abbreviations whose character length is 3, an exception to the previous rule.

Equation tokenization creates an effective vocabulary by converting equations into SLT format, collecting collection wide frequency statistics, and including all equation units whose frequency count is greater than INLINEFORM0.

Held out sets are generated for each equation by randomly sampling words from its context set, including sampled words, their context window with the equation, negative samples, and a validation set; for each of the INLINEFORM0 equations, two held out words INLINEFORM1 are sampled, with context window size 4 defined as INLINEFORM2.

During training, predictive log-likelihood on the validation set is computed after each iteration using a fitted model of interaction and feature vectors, with held out word log probability computed by DISPLAYFORM0.

The formula is the softmax over negative samples INLINEFORM0 and the held out word; the model ran 20 times across the collection, stopping at the INLINEFORM3-th iteration when predictive log-likelihood no longer improves over the previous INLINEFORM2 iteration.
EqEmb modeling uses two passes: first modeling words while ignoring equations, then modeling equations while holding fixed word interaction and feature vectors, treating equations as singleton words.

EqEmb models were evaluated across word context (W), word-equation context (E) and embedding vector size (K), compared with b-emb, CBOW, GloVe and PV-DM, using gensim BIBREF13 for CBOW and PV-DM and separate paragraph labels for PV-DM equation contexts.
Table TABREF23 compares embedding models on K=25, 50, 75 and 100, Word Context=4, 8 and 16, E=8 and 16 for EqEmb, EqEmb-U and PV-DM, using pseudo log-likelihood BIBREF14 defined as DISPLAYFORM0.
This is treated as a downstream task, with the validation set selecting the best model configuration for each model type and latent dimension configuration, and values reported on both datasets.
Across all collections EqEmb outperform previous embedding models and EqEmb-U further improves performance.

EqEmb help obtain word descriptions of equations, with Table TABREF25 showing an example equation and the 5 most similar words from CBOW, PV-DM, GloVe and EqEmb using Cosine distance between INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1.

Equation search using words as queries averages word embedding representations and computes Cosine distance across equation embeddings, with Table TABREF25 showing a three-word query and its 5 nearest equations discovered using EqEmb.

EqEmb models capture semantic similarity between equations, with qualitative analysis over all discovered equations across the 4 collection, Table TABREF24 showing the query equation and its 5 most similar equations using EqEmb-U, Appendix A comparisons with CBOW, PV-DM, GloVe and EqEmb, tab:irexample1,tab:nlpexample2 showing additional examples, Cosine distance for similar words, Euclidean distance for similar equations, and additional results in Appendix B.

The paper presented unsupervised approaches for semantic representations of mathematical equations using surrounding words, showed more effective modeling across 4 different collections, demonstrated semantic similarity between equations and words, and plans to explore EqEmb for images, captions and inline figures.
